01 / DECISION

Decision Brief

Start with the decision—not the meeting. Define the commitment being considered, the current boundary, who owns it, and what evidence could legitimately change it.

A position should move because the facts, alternatives, dependencies, timing, or risk allocation changed—not because the room became uncomfortable.
02 / LEVERAGE

Counterparty + Leverage Map

Apply Dependency vs. Leverage. Model what each side says, needs, controls, fears, and faces if no agreement occurs.

QuestionUsCounterparty
Stated position
Underlying interest
Constraint / must-have
Alternative state if no deal
Authority / approvals
Urgency / time pressure
Dependency
Leverage we can actually exercise
Cost of no agreement
Leverage is not who wants the deal less. It is who controls the terms, alternatives, timing, or downside the other side cannot easily replace.
03 / EVIDENCE

Evidence + Learning Agenda

Apply Signal vs. Narrative. Separate verified facts from supported beliefs, assumptions, and unknowns. Each meeting should close a decision-relevant information gap.

Issue / claimStatusEvidence or observed signalDecision-changing question

Learning test

04 / TIMING

Timing + Process Architecture

Apply Timing Asymmetry. Before negotiating harder, ask whether sequence, access, deadlines, competition, or commitment architecture should change.

Time is valuable only when it creates information, preserves optionality, or shifts dependency. Delay without one of those effects is not strategy.
05 / EXCHANGE

Terms + Value Exchange

Map differences before bargaining one term at a time. Look for things that are cheap to one side, valuable to the other, or capable of reallocating risk more efficiently than price alone.

Issue / termValue to usValue to themCost to usCost to themRisk / dependency transferred
Never negotiate a term in isolation if another term can buy it cheaper.
06 / LEDGER

Concession + Decision Ledger

Make movement inspectable. Record why the position changed, what value moved in each direction, and how the development changes the M&A decision record.

Methodology + provenance

How the record works

The Negotiation Decision Record is an original MikeYe.com decision-support object. It does not score negotiating “skill” or prescribe scripts. It converts negotiation into an auditable M&A decision record: the decision, evidence, conditions, unknowns, leverage, timing, terms, concessions, consequence, owner, next action, and gate.

Ontology

The record operationalizes the existing MikeYe.com judgment lenses: Dependency vs. Leverage, Timing Asymmetry, Signal vs. Narrative, and Scarcity vs. Growth. Material developments resolve into the existing M&A consequence vocabulary: Investigate / Price / Protect / Walk, followed by the gate decision: Advance / Hold-Rework / Walk.

Research lineage

The design is informed by durable negotiation research on interests and alternatives, process architecture, value creation, disciplined concessions, behavioral bias, anchoring, and perspective-taking. The research is adapted here only where it maps to transaction judgment; the operating system, vocabulary, and decision record are MikeYe.com’s.

Influences reviewed: Harvard Negotiation Project; David Lax & James Sebenius; Deepak Malhotra; Max Bazerman; Adam Galinsky; Robert Mnookin; Leigh Thompson; Chris Voss.

Limitations

This is a decision-support framework, not legal, tax, valuation, fiduciary, or transaction advice. It cannot know information that has not been entered and does not determine whether a deal is “good.” The quality of the output depends on the quality of the evidence and the discipline of distinguishing fact from assumption.

Privacy by design.
Deal inputs in this version stay in your browser through local storage. They are not submitted to MikeYe.com. Export JSON if you want a portable machine-readable record; Print / Save PDF creates a human-readable snapshot.

Decision rule

Increase commitment only when uncertainty has fallen, risk has been priced or protected, or the alternative state has materially changed.
